byKey.lam: 2 is the variance of the PC2 score, $(A - B)/\sqrt2$. The spread $A - B$ is $\sqrt2$ times that, so its variance is twice as big.
byKey.plus: You added the covariance term. It enters with a minus sign for a difference.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def low_rank(A, k):
    A = np.asarray(A, dtype=float)
    U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False)
    return U[:, :k] @ np.diag(s[:k]) @ Vt[:k, :]

items.title: Hedging a gilt book with two components
items.prompt: PCA of 15 days of gilt yield changes gave eigenvalues 36.08, 7.16, 1.36, 0.09 and 0.02. The yields are the 2y, 5y, 10y, 20y and 30y, in bp. To 2 decimal places, PC1 has loadings $(0.42, 0.43, 0.44, 0.45, 0.49)$ and PC2 has $(-0.45, -0.49, -0.14, 0.27, 0.68)$. A book's P&L for a 1 bp rise in each yield is $\mathbf{s} = (-100, -200, -300, -200, -100)$ £. (a) Find the book's exposures $e_1 = \mathbf{s}\cdot\mathbf{v}_1$ and $e_2 = \mathbf{s}\cdot\mathbf{v}_2$. (b) PC scores are uncorrelated with variances $\lambda_i$. Find the standard deviation of daily P&L from PC1 and PC2 together. (c) You add a 2y position with sensitivity $a$ £ per bp and a 30y position with sensitivity $b$. Find $a$ and $b$ that make both exposures zero. (d) Explain why hedging two components beats hedging five yields one by one, and give two risks that remain.
items.model:
**(a)** $e_1 = -100(0.42) - 200(0.43) - 300(0.44) - 200(0.45) - 100(0.49) = -42 - 86 - 132 - 90 - 49 = -399$ £ per unit of PC1. $e_2 = -100(-0.45) - 200(-0.49) - 300(-0.14) - 200(0.27) - 100(0.68) = 45 + 98 + 42 - 54 - 68 = 63$ £ per unit of PC2.

**(b)** P&L from the two components is $e_1z_1 + e_2z_2$ with $z_1, z_2$ uncorrelated. Its variance is $\lambda_1e_1^2 + \lambda_2e_2^2 = 36.08(399^2) + 7.16(63^2) = 5{,}743{,}972 + 28{,}418 = 5{,}772{,}390$. The standard deviation is $\sqrt{5{,}772{,}390} \approx$ £2,403 a day. PC1 alone gives $\sqrt{36.08} \times 399 \approx$ £2,397: the level move is almost all of the risk.

**(c)** The 2y position adds $0.42a$ to $e_1$ and $-0.45a$ to $e_2$; the 30y adds $0.49b$ and $0.68b$. Set both totals to zero: $$\begin{aligned} 0.42a + 0.49b &= 399, \\ -0.45a + 0.68b &= -63. \end{aligned}$$ The determinant is $0.42(0.68) + 0.49(0.45) = 0.5061$. Cramer's rule gives $a = (399 \times 0.68 - 0.49 \times (-63))/0.5061 = 302.19/0.5061 \approx 597$ and $b = (0.42 \times (-63) + 0.45 \times 399)/0.5061 = 153.09/0.5061 \approx 302.5$. Both are positive. They are short positions that gain when yields rise. That is about £597 per bp at 2y and £302 per bp at 30y. Check: $0.42(597) + 0.49(302.5) = 250.7 + 148.2 = 399$ and $-0.45(597) + 0.68(302.5) = -268.7 + 205.7 = -63$.

**(d)** Five yields move together, so five separate hedges would hedge the same level move five times, with five instruments. PC1 and PC2 explain $(36.08 + 7.16)/44.71 = 96.7\%$ of the variance, so two instruments remove almost all of it. Four risks remain:

- Curvature and the smaller components carry 3.3% of the variance, and the hedged book stays exposed to them.
- The loadings come from only 15 days and change over time, so the hedge drifts.
- A sign or ordering slip in the PCA hedges the wrong component: `eigh`'s first column, or an unfixed sign.
- The hedge ignores carry, the basis between futures and bonds, and large non-linear moves.

rubric.text: Computes $e_1 = -399$ and $e_2 = 63$ (allow small rounding) as dot products of sensitivities with loadings.
Uses $\lambda_1e_1^2 + \lambda_2e_2^2$ for the variance, citing uncorrelated scores, and gets about £2,400.
Sets up the two hedge equations correctly and solves them, $a \approx 597$ and $b \approx 302$, with a check.
Explains why two components suffice, citing the 96.7% share or the common level move.
Names at least two remaining risks, such as PC3, unstable loadings or basis.
